newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says Ramos needs surgery but not critical.
newsitem.headline: Manila says Ramos needs surgery but not critical.

text.p: Philippines President Fidel Ramos is more ill than previously believed and may require heart surgery, officials said on Monday.
"As of now, we cannot confirm yet if the president will have to undergo surgery because he is still being examined," presidential Press Secretary Hector Villanueva said in a statement.
The statement said medical tests were being conducted and the cabinet would be briefed on Ramos's health at 9 a.m. (0100 GMT) but gave no further details.

Ramos, 68, was admitted to hospital for the second time in 10 days on Sunday and doctors initially said he was to undergo further checks after being confined to bed with a throat infection the previous weekend.

But television reports said on Sunday evening that doctors suspected an artery blockage and that the president was to undergo an angiography test. If necessary, the test would be followed by surgery, the reports said.
Angiography is an X-ray test which uses an injected opaque dye to show up blocked arteries.
Ramos set off alarm bells on Manila's bourse and corporate boardrooms when he was admitted to the hospital on December 12 and some newspapers reported he had suffered a mild stroke.
He was released three days later after being treated for what doctors said was a throat infection.
Ramos resumed a heavy schedule of speaking engagements and other public appearances shortly after he checked out, apparently to scotch the rumours of serious ill-health.
Doctors urged him to slow down and Ramos cancelled a series of provincial trips.
He told his weekly news conference on Wednesday he was in good health and that jitters in the stock market over his health appeared to be over.

Ramos's hospital spells coincided with a controversy over calls by a citizens' group to amend the constitution to allow him to run for re-election when his six-year term ends in June 1998. The constitution limits a president to a single term.
